title: The Test Stack: Typecheck as Contract, Tests as Behavior — Check

questions.prompt: What does `npm run typecheck` verify that `npm test` does not?
questions.explanation: The type checker enforces structural contracts at compile time, flagging every consumer when a signature changes — a form of contract checking distinct from behavioral tests.
options: That the runtime behavior produces correct numeric results
That argument and return shapes line up across the gateway and domain modules, surfacing contract drift everywhere a module is used
That the production redirects are configured correctly
That the AI mock returns deterministic responses

questions.prompt: Why does keeping logic in `netlify/lib/*` and thin wrappers in `netlify/functions/*` make the suite faster?
questions.explanation: With logic in importable modules, tests invoke functions directly and avoid network/runtime overhead, leaving only a few integration tests for the wrappers.
options: Because TypeScript compiles faster with more files
Because most logic can be unit-tested by calling library functions directly, without the Netlify runtime, HTTP, or redirects
Because thin wrappers cannot contain bugs
Because Netlify functions cannot be tested at all

questions.prompt: Passing `npm run typecheck` is sufficient on its own to prove the gateway's logic is correct.
questions.explanation: Types prove shapes align but not that the logic computes the right values or routes correctly; behavioral tests in `npm test` are still required.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible reason to run `npm run typecheck && npm test` in that order in CI?
questions.explanation: Running the fast, codebase-wide consistency check first gives quick feedback on shape mismatches before investing time in behavioral tests.
options: Tests must always run before typechecking
The cheap, broad typecheck fails fast on contract drift before the slower behavioral tests run
Typecheck depends on the production deployment
It is the only order Netlify supports
